name: Liam Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is your ordinary day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, a senior carpenter fitting curved acoustic ceiling panels in a new concert hall. I hold a vocational trade certificate and supervise the panel lift, set out the ribs and make sure the sprinkler openings are clear. The finished curve is satisfying; protecting people below a suspended panel is the hard responsibility.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are pay, home and AI use for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My specialist site rate is high, and similar construction jobs are plentiful nearby. My partner works at a clinic, our children are grown, and we have eleven months of expenses saved. I hope to finish paid work at 67 if our income allows. I use AI now and then for draft timber orders, but check its numbers against the real ribs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the joinery crew a modest AI improvement can help with ordering curved timber, but the concert hall ceiling still has to be fitted to its real supports. I'm content to use the estimate as a starting point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My senior carpenter rate is high and comparable jobs are plentiful around here. My partner works in a clinic, our children are grown, and we have eleven months of expenses saved. I'd like to leave site work at 67 if our income covers it; this mild outcome keeps that possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on fitting the hall's curved acoustic panels and use AI occasionally to draft order notes, as I already do. I'll check its quantities against measured ribs and keep putting fresh money from each wage into our savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The tool saves a little paper time, my paid carpentry hours remain, and I can see the finished ceiling taking shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the drawing fail on this job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A panel that looks identical on a drawing can need a different cut where a sprinkler crosses the rib. We mark the actual obstruction before ordering another piece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you decide when to stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 67 we'd count our real income and expenses before I stop. Our savings help us plan retirement, but I still need carpentry wages until our household can afford to stop.

think: My **high carpenter wage** carries on in the mild case.
Eleven months of **expenses saved** support a conditional age-67 retirement.
do: **Continue** fitting concert hall panels and measuring hidden crossings.
**Add** new savings from each wage while using occasional AI drafts.
feel: **Calm** about steady paid work and modest paperwork gains.

steps.text: Keep fitting and measuring curved hall ceiling panels
Add new money from each wage to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI may speed design revisions, but management has to leave paid time for us to check the curves. I'd support a union request for proper instruction before anyone is asked to approve a machine drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may send us more revised panels in a week, but I don't expect my own wage to shrink yet. I am willing to try a proved tool that reduces rework, provided the crew can still reject a bad quantity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for access to the updated drawing tool with a paid instructor and try its revision controls on one unused ceiling bay if that supervised slot is offered. If it behaves, I'll learn how to mark the sprinkler clash and show the corrections to the site manager. I'll back the union's request for paid checking time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about rushed revisions, though my hours look safe. I've changed tools before once they worked on a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What conditions would make a tool trial safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test bay must be closed to other trades, with the panel supported and an experienced carpenter beside the instructor. I am requesting a paid drawing-tool trial in a closed ceiling bay; nobody has offered me a place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the revised cut list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the revised cut list with our hand measurements and ask the manager to keep a sign-off point. If the tool misses the crossing, I will keep the manual marking method for that panel.

A **closed test bay** lets carpenters check a panel without exposing other trades.
think: My **wage looks secure**, although faster revisions could squeeze inspection time.

do: **Request** a paid supervised trial on an unused ceiling bay.
**Learn** revision controls if a safe trial and instructor are offered.
**Support** the union request for paid checking time.
feel: **Uneasy** about revision pressure, while paid hours remain secure.
S1.quote: I am requesting a paid drawing-tool trial in a closed ceiling bay; nobody has offered me a place yet.
fieldNote: The **paid trial** is a request, while learning controls depends on an offered supervised place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 could redesign the ceiling before we touch it, and capable site robots around 2031 might fit repetitive panels. We should demand proof of safe lifting and real paid places for the people whose installation hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, four years short of my hoped-for age-67 exit. Eleven months of savings gives us room, and local construction jobs are plentiful, but a sharp reduction in my higher wage would still change our retirement sums. I can adapt if the alternative work pays enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask our union steward for a written crew plan and paid practical rigging course with a real place, supervised lifts and a recognized qualification. If offered, I'll attend while keeping my wage. If our panel hours are cut after I qualify, I'll apply for posted local robot-rigging roles where the advertised wage, safe duties and hours meet our household need; without a course, I'd apply for posted local carpentry jobs that pay enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage cut, even with strong savings. I would rather learn the safe lift and move to an actual vacancy than burn through our reserve waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should rigging training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course must teach us to secure a curved panel when the suction head loses pressure, and a qualified supervisor has to stop the rig. An automation brochure cannot teach a safe ceiling-panel lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you choose between a rigging and carpentry job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the advertised rigging rate with my current pay and our expected costs. If the new role pays less than we need, I'll take a suitable posted carpentry job instead of assuming a new title is a safer retirement route.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may redesign ceilings before robots fit panels around 2031.
Workers need **paid safe lifting instruction** and a clear crew plan.
think: At **63**, a lower wage could disrupt a conditional age-67 exit.
Eleven months of **savings** and plentiful local work provide time to choose.
do: **Seek** paid recognized rigging instruction with supervised lifts.
**Apply** for posted local robot-rigging work after qualifying if hours are cut.
**Apply** if no paid course to posted local carpentry jobs with enough pay; keep earning while training terms are checked.
feel: **Anxious** about a real threat to higher pay close to retirement.
S2.quote: An automation brochure cannot teach a safe ceiling-panel lift.
fieldNote: Training requires an **offered paid place**, supervised practice and recognized qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI changes design around 2031 and robots fit panels around 2034, we have five years to test a lift properly. I'd tell the crew to insist that a human signs off each support before a robot raises a panel over anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when the hands-on machines appear, one year before I hope to stop. Our strong reserve is useful, but I cannot claim I will be retired until we've checked actual income. A shortened final year's roster could still cost us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working on the hall and ask for a paid supervised rigging place if the contractor develops robot lifts. If a recognized course is offered with wages, I'll enrol and practise emergency stops on an empty bay. If I still need to work at 66 and panel hours are cut, I'll apply after qualification to posted local rigging jobs with adequate pay and safe duties; otherwise I'll keep the current paid carpentry work until our exit is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the machine arrives close to my planned exit. Five years lets us check our income and gives the contractor time to offer real training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe test lift include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a test lift I would sling the panel to a certified point, mark the exclusion zone and cut power if the head loses pressure. I won't practise over a live walkway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still apply if you can retire at 67?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our income supports stopping at 67, I will retire instead of seeking a fresh post. If it does not, a real posted salary and safe hours decide whether moving from the panel crew makes sense.

Each **support point** needs a human check before a robot raises a load.
think: At **66**, I may still need one more year of higher site pay.
My **age-67 exit** depends on actual household income, despite strong savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI reaches building design in 2036 and capable robots fit panels around 2039, I'll tell the union we have time to settle lifting standards before anyone stands below a robot. The curved hall bays show why identical plans cannot settle a real load path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and about 71 when robots work overhead. I hope to leave paid site work at 67 if our income allows, so I may have retired before either change affects my own roster. If we still need my wage, I would not want late-career hours cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the present higher paid carpentry work, add fresh savings from each wage and review our age-67 income target annually. I'll share the hall's tested lifting checks with the union safety committee. If I still need work after 67 and robots cut my site hours, I'll apply to posted local jobs I qualify for with safe duties and enough stated pay, whether they involve carpentry or supervised lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the younger trades and mildly concerned about my own possible exposure if retirement slips. The long delay gives us time to improve the savings and check actual vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What record would you leave the next crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall lift record shows the support point, exclusion zone and pressure test, not just a tidy model. I'll leave that record with the site safety team so they can inspect the next curved bay properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if income at 67 falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each year my partner and I will compare real spending with expected income. At sixty-seven I stop paid work only if household income covers spending; otherwise I keep earning and check safe local vacancies with sufficient pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which scenario worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 fast change worries me most because robots around 2031 could reduce my specialist hours at 63. A paid recognized rigging place, safe supervised practice and a real local vacancy with enough pay would give me a route if the roster shrinks.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who stops a lift when the suction head loses pressure above the hall floor. A ceiling panel has to be secured before anyone walks underneath it.

headlineQuote: A ceiling panel has to be secured before anyone walks underneath it.
portrait: **Liam**, 58, is a high-paid senior carpenter with a vocational trade certificate, fitting curved concert hall panels.
He and his clinic-worker partner have grown children and **eleven months** of household expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for draft orders, checks the site measurements, and waits for proven tools.
He hopes to stop at **67** if income permits and would seek paid rigging training if robots shorten his roster.
biggestWorry: **Fast site robots** around 2031 could reduce his specialist hours at 63, affecting the conditional age-67 plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid recognized rigging place**, supervised lift practice and a suitable posted local job at sufficient pay.
